disease_info: Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type) is characterized by a combination of psychotic symptoms (such as delusions and hallucinations) and mood episodes meeting full criteria for mania, with or without major depressive episodes, where psychotic symptoms also occur for at least two weeks in the absence of prominent mood symptoms. The course is typically chronic or episodic with periods of partial remission, and functional impairment is common in social and occupational domains. It is distinguished from bipolar disorder with psychotic features by the presence of psychosis outside of mood episodes, and from schizophrenia by the prominence and duration of mood episodes over the illness course. Onset is often in late adolescence or early adulthood but can emerge later in the context of psychosocial stressors, substance use, or medical comorbidity, especially in individuals with a pre-existing vulnerability.

narrative.personality: A steady, pragmatic caregiver who enjoys quiet, hands-on hobbies and mindfulness, and who values routine while remaining curious and improvisational in problem-solving.
narrative.stressor: About three years ago, Jimmy decided to push himself professionally by enrolling in evening classes to prepare for his Certified Nursing Assistant credential while continuing full-time work as a personal care aide. The added academic demands, tighter documentation requirements at his agency, and pressure he put on himself to become a supervisor gradually eroded the balance he had maintained through gardening, fishing, and meditation. As his workload increased, he began taking on extra shifts to impress his supervisors, sleeping less and neglecting his usual grounding routines, which coincided with periods of unusually high energy and grand plans for overhauling care at his facility, followed by marked crashes in motivation and self-doubt. Over the next 2 years and 5 months, his ability to stay organized deteriorated, he became inconsistent at work, missed deadlines for his CNA coursework, and grew increasingly distressed by unusual experiences that he could no longer explain away; his wife and a long-term client finally urged him to seek psychiatric care after he admitted that these experiences were starting to interfere with his ability to safely care for patients.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I keep seeing and hearing things that I know aren’t really there, and it’s scaring me.”

narrative.personality: A calm, detail-oriented young woman who enjoys structured, quiet pastimes like gardening, knitting, and puzzles, and who takes pride in providing steady, patient customer service.
narrative.stressor: Michele’s difficulties began shortly after a cluster of major changes: she married her long-term boyfriend, moved out of her parents’ home into a small apartment, and transitioned from part-time to full-time work at the department store, all within a few months. Initially she felt energized and eager to prove she could manage a household and full-time job, taking on extra shifts, planning elaborate meals, and trying to keep the apartment picture-perfect while also maintaining her hobbies. Over the following year, this heightened drive became increasingly difficult to control, with stretches where she stayed up nearly all night organizing, planning projects, and starting new hobbies, followed by periods where she felt overwhelmed, guilty, and unable to enjoy the very routines she used to find soothing. As this pattern persisted over more than two years and began to affect her reliability at work, her marriage, and her sense of reality, her husband and manager both expressed concern, and Michele finally agreed to see a psychiatrist when she realized she was regularly functioning on only a few hours of sleep yet feeling strangely overcharged and unable to slow down.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Lately I only sleep a couple of hours a night and still feel wired, like I don’t need sleep at all.”

narrative.personality: A curious, creative young man who combines meticulous work with spontaneous artistic pursuits, balancing structured budgeting habits with occasional impulsive indulgence in art and music.
narrative.stressor: Brian’s problems emerged toward the end of his first year working as an accounting clerk, when long-standing tensions at home escalated after his parents’ separation and his father’s abrupt move out of state. Trying to help his mother manage finances while working full-time, he initially threw himself into both responsibilities, spending late nights perfecting reports and then sketching or going to shows to blow off steam, feeling unusually driven and confident about fixing everything. Over time, the strain of shifting family roles, unresolved anger toward his father, and his own high expectations led to increasingly erratic cycles of intense productivity and withdrawal, and his once-enjoyable solitary activities like hiking and journaling began to be overshadowed by bleak ruminations about failure and the pointlessness of his efforts. Over the next 2 years and 5 months, his functioning at work and in his volunteer tutoring declined, he became socially isolated, and his thoughts about death grew more frequent and detailed, culminating in him seeking psychiatric help after confiding to a close friend that he had started planning ways to end his life.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’ve been thinking a lot about dying lately, and it’s getting to the point where I’m scared of what I might do.”
